implementation_notes: Java's route to a memento is an immutable value type: a record is a transparent carrier whose components are final and exposed only through accessors, so the snapshot class is one line and the caretaker is a Deque<State> (ArrayDeque) with a bounded size - undo is an assignment. Records are only shallowly immutable, though: a component that is a mutable List or array lets callers mutate the snapshot through its accessor, so the compact constructor must copy (List.copyOf, Arrays.copyOf) or the components must themselves be immutable. The classic nested-class Memento is still justified when the snapshot must stay private to the originator rather than being a public value.
pitfalls: Records are shallowly immutable: a List or array component is shared with every holder of the snapshot and can be mutated through the accessor - copy defensively in a compact canonical constructor.
An unbounded Deque keeps whole state graphs alive; the JDK's own UndoManager has a setLimit for exactly this reason, so a hand-rolled history needs its own bound.

Serializable deep copies are slow and deserializing untrusted streams is an attack surface; if snapshots are persisted, prefer explicit DTOs or JSON over Java serialization, or apply serialization filters (JEP 290).
Records define equals/hashCode over all components, so a snapshot used as a map key must have stable, hashable state (deep-copy mutable components or avoid mutable ones).

variants.name: javax.swing.undo.UndoManager as the caretaker
variants.implementation_notes: The JDK ships the caretaker: UndoManager keeps an ordered list of UndoableEdit records with an index of the next edit, supports undo and redo, discards the redo tail when a new edit arrives, and can bound the history with setLimit (the default is effectively unlimited). UndoableEdit is change-based - it records how to invert an action (AbstractUndoableEdit, CompoundEdit for grouped changes) rather than a whole-state snapshot - so use it when the inverse of a change is cheaper and more precise than copying the state, and keep record snapshots inside an edit when you want the memento semantics. It lives in java.desktop, so it costs a Swing module on server-side code.
pitfalls: Adding an edit after an undo discards the redo tail (each discarded edit receives die()), so mixing your own history list with the manager corrupts the index bookkeeping.
The manager is unbounded unless setLimit is called; a UI that never trims history keeps every edit alive.
UndoableEdit models change inversion, not state capture: a badly written edit can drift from the real state, so commands whose inverse is lossy need a snapshot instead.
java.desktop is part of the platform but not of a minimal server image; a headless service pulling in Swing for undo is a smell.

variants.name: Serializable round-trip deep copies
variants.implementation_notes: The long-standing Java deep-copy trick is to serialize the state to a byte array and read it back: ObjectOutputStream writes the reachable graph, ObjectInputStream reconstructs an independent one, so a snapshot is a byte[] and restore deserializes and copies the fields back. It handles arbitrary graphs (cycles, shared references) without writing copy code, and the same bytes can be persisted, which makes it the cheap path to durable history - at the cost of requiring every class in the state to be Serializable, of being markedly slower than copying fields, and of inheriting the deserialization attack surface.
pitfalls: Unpickling runs readObject on attacker-influenced data - never restore mementos from untrusted sources, and prefer serialization filters (JEP 290) when the bytes cross a boundary.
Every class involved must be Serializable with a stable serialVersionUID, otherwise snapshots break on recompilation; a changed field layout silently yields nulls or InvalidClassException.
The round-trip is orders of magnitude slower than field copying and doubles peak memory, so it suits checkpoints and persisted history rather than per-keystroke undo.
transient fields are deliberately excluded; the originator must rebuild whatever it marked transient when restoring.
